The initial state \(|3,0,0\rangle\) (3s) decays to the ground state \(|1,0,0\rangle\) (1s) via two electric dipole transitions. Due to dipole selection rules (\(\Delta l = \pm 1\)), the only allowed first step is to the \(2p\) state (\(n=2, l=1\)). The intermediate state can have \(m = -1, 0, +1\).

From the initial \(m=0\) state, the three possible dipole transitions to \(|2,1,m\rangle\) have equal partial decay rates because the squared matrix elements \(|\langle 2,1,m| r_q |3,0,0\rangle|^2\) summed over photon polarizations \(q\) are identical for all \(m\). Therefore the branching ratio to each \(m\) sublevel is \(1/3\).

The second step \(|2,1,m\rangle \to |1,0,0\rangle\) is the only dipole-allowed decay for the \(2p\) state, so it occurs with unit probability for each \(m\). Thus the overall probability for the cascade path \(|3,0,0\rangle \to |2,1,0\rangle \to |1,0,0\rangle\) is \(1/3\). (The common mistake of doubling this probability to \(2/3\) corresponds to option (A).)
